utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Good morning to the Defence. Together with co-counsel Joanne Richardson and our case manager Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Vasvija Vidovic together with Mr. John Jones, appearing on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Miss Adisa Mehic and our case manager Mr. Geoff Roberts. Good morning also to my learned friends from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good morning to your team. Any preliminaries before I say mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have over the weekend had a family matter arising that needs attending to with some -- not exactly urgency but it needs to be attended to before -- definitely before -- that is, the sooner the better. And so I need to go home for two days, and the only flights that I have managed to secure is leaving on the 19th of May which means basically the two sittings of the 19th and 20th will have to go and we'll have to make up for those later on. So I will of course be returning the same weekend so I leave Thursday and I come back Saturday or Sunday. I mean I'm wait-listed both going out and coming in so I don't know exactly what's going to happen but that's the position. So the 19th and the 20th. There is one witness scheduled for those two days, and we will have to reschedule that witness. Basically that's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that Mr. Wubben. I thought of letting you know straight away. All the flights are pretty booked and overbooked and I had a big problems trying to find a flight to go home. So let's bring the witness in and continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Okanovic. I hope you had a good weekend here in The Hague, in this beautiful city of The Hague, and we will now proceed with your testimony and you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just two matters. May I please remind you that you are testifying under oath pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made last Friday; and that secondly, since we depend to a large extent if not completely on interpretation here, if at any time there are problems with your receiving interpretation, please draw our attention straight away, because we need to be able to follow the testimony and everyone else needs to be able to follow the testimony in all the languages of this Tribunal. So I thank you. Good morning, and Mr. Jones may start with his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And good morning from me, Mr. Okanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You speak English?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to start by revisiting the video which you were shown on Friday just in one or two parts to fill in some gaps. Now, firstly, I'll indicate beforehand what I'm going to ask you to look out for and the first thing it's a very small thing but on the transcript, P316.1, we have a name appearing, Razo. It says "Razo" on the transcript. I'm going to play the segment and tell us if you actually here the name "Raso." So if we could just play starting at 3120.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible it might be Raso. It might be. "Raso told me so," that might be what they are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Raso is a Serb name, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it short for Radovan?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we are going to play another segment and if you could tell us this time if you hear the words I'll say it in Bosnian. [B/C/S spoken] or perhaps [B/C/S spoken]. We'll play the segment starting at 3232.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's someone standing next to me commenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that essentially means look how well the plane is bombing or blasting or something of that nature? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite agree with the blasting. This wasn't something that we could see. We could only hear explosions and we didn't know exactly what they were hitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just on the transcript, firstly, that appears as "Look how well he's flying." You agree that that's not what was being said by the person next to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken] refers to throwing rockets or bombs or some projectile?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Next, do you recall that you said at some point in response to a question, "ours went silent." [B/C/S spoken]. Do you recall that from Friday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do but I don't remember what the reason was for saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll play that segment and that starts at 3320.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you hear yourself saying something of that nature in that section?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard my own voice. A person standing next to me was asking me whether it was Miko. I said I had no idea and then my voice says, "He came back without having done anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. In particular I wanted to ask you about this expression which it appears -- well, which you commented on Friday, that "Ours went silent" and when you were asked about that you said that you were referring to Bosnian Serb soldiers. For the sake of clarity I'll refer to the transcript from Friday and it's page 17 lines 2 to 7 in LiveNote. And you said: "Witness: Again, this young boy is asking me who is firing and I'm replying, well, it's not our men because our men weren't shooting. That's what I told him. And when I said 'our men,' -- the transcript is a bit unclear but the reference was Bosnian Serbs. And then Your Honour pointed out the statement was made at 34.561. It's that I want to ask you about now. Now, on Friday you told us repeatedly that you couldn't see any people in Sikiric that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was not able to see any people there, from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the Prosecution asked you if you saw Bosnian Serb soldiers that day and you said no. Isn't it right that in effect that question is misleading because you didn't see anybody that day, Muslims, Serbs, soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right. I saw no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, just while we are on this theme, how far roughly is the distance from your house to Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you also told us how later you went down to the Drina and looked across and you still couldn't see people. What distance would that be from where you were by the Drina over to Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 300 or 400 metres from the Drina. I was able to see some houses that were nearby but I did not see any persons. If I had seen any persons I would have taped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that from 500 metres, or thereabouts, it's not actually possible to see whether someone is wearing a uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to clarify something. It didn't mean anything to us at the time, seeing someone in civilian clothes or in uniform. People just wore uniforms. Those were no textbook armies on either side. Those people were just civilians heading off to war. A uniform meant nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and if I can follow up on that, is it correct then that if you saw someone in civilian clothes they could be a soldier, firstly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be, but I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just speaking about in general terms, the army as you described it in this period, on both sides. Secondly, that someone could be wearing a uniform or a piece of uniform and not be a soldier but simply possess a uniform from their military service? You have to give a verbal answer, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't your run-of-the-mill army, like I said. Those were just armed civilians on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally on this theme, can you confirm that farmers would sometimes wear bits of uniform just because they were well made and warm rather than because they were serving in a unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's true of both sides, Muslim and Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You see that sort of thing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back, then, to what we heard about "ours went silent" and your reference to the fact that as you put it, your men weren't shooting. Since you couldn't see any people, in fact, you didn't know who was shooting, did you, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the plane probably, I'm not even sure myself what I meant. One thing is certain, I couldn't see anyone at the time but I probably had the plane in mind when I said that. Something to the effect that it just flew by without firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Flew by on that occasion without firing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you accept that in terms of who was shooting at whom, you didn't know whether it was Serbs or Muslims who was doing the firing.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, your answer wasn't translated. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do accept that, yes. There was no way I could know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could it be also that when you were referring to "ours went" -- this phrase, "ours went silent," you could be referring to artillery in Serbia which had ceased shooting at that moment or -- let me put that a different way. Isn't it right that there was artillery in Serbia, in Ljubovija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time. I'm sure about that. Had there been any armed forces on the Serbian side, we would not have needed to organise any village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. But do you accept that there was heavy artillery in Ljubovija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like with respect to counsel's question -- exactly when, at what time period is he referring to. Are we talking about the day in question or prior to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it we are talking about the day in question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I can go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said at that time. "No, not at that time." There wasn't artillery in Serbia. So at what time was there or what time did you become aware that there was --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question is did at any later point in time then was there artillery in the location that was mentioned to you by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, in Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I only know that later on some armed forces arrived of the Republika Srpska or Yugoslavia but I don't know when exactly. But that was much later. I can't be sure about when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I may come back to that but thank you for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about an expression we heard on the video where on the transcript it appears you don't know which is which and I want you to listen to the segment and see whether that's what you hear or whether you hear you don't know who is who. [B/C/S spoken]. So we'll play that segment which starts at 3510.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you were saying you don't know who was who?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was someone next to me who suggested that we go and help them and I said who are you going to help, if you don't know who was who? They are both wearing the same kind of uniform. Now who are you going to be helping? There was no way you to distinguish soldiers on the basis of where they belonged and there was no way you could tell their accents either. That was the meaning behind my words. I said you don't know who is who, not meaning anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was based on your general knowledge of how things were, that it appeared to you a scene of complete confusion and chaos on the other side of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And into this scene, as we've seen the Serb planes were dropping bombs, did you hear that -- did you hear after the action that some Serbs were killed by bombs dropped by Serb planes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I heard is that Muslim forces had killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it not be consistent with what you saw, this chaotic scene, that people were actually killed by bombs as well, Serbs and Muslims alike?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the manner in which this question is being posed. I think the witness answered the question. If Mr. Jones would put the question in a different way, whether or not he's aware or he observed bombs killing these individuals, that's another question. But the way in which he posed it whatever answer the witness gives may be misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you Ms. Richardson. Could you rephrase your question if you wish to pursue the matter, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I won't pursue the matter. It was really to do with what he heard rather than what he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the next section I'd like you to list hear and listen if you hear persons saying ours are doing very well. [B/C/S spoken] and [B/C/S spoken], and that's starting from 3800 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, can you confirm that's what you heard.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is someone commenting over the radio. They are referring to the bird, probably meaning the plane, and they are saying that it did a good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in general, that's an expression of the fact that the Serb side is doing well at that time, at least that the airplanes are doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't take my word for it. I think you should just listen and try to see for yourself. There was no way I could see from where I was whether someone was doing a good job for not. Therefore I don't think I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: For a question of clarification, if the question it was asked as -- that the airplanes are doing their job. Now, the remark which was made, was it made with regard to both planes in the morning and the afternoon or was it referring to one plane only? And if so, which planes, the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was at 10.00 in the morning. He says the bird in the singular did well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So at that time there was only one plane? Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall, but the person speaking on the radio says the bird did well. He's referring to a plane in the singular.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a reference to one plane but you're not saying, are you, that you know there was only one plane in the air at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I looked at the tape the second time, it was only then I noticed that there were two planes. I don't recall there being two. It was only when I looked at the tape again that I realised that there were two different planes. I don't have this tape at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this up because I think there is a little bit of confusion now. We saw the tape last Friday and I agree with you that on that tape, at least, there are two distinctly different planes, one is just a biplane, with two layers of wings and the other one is just an ordinary propeller-driven plane. Were they flying -- were they in the sky together at any given time during the day that you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall. Had they been there both together I would probably have taped that. I don't recall that they were there together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just on that subject I'll come back to it but the biplane was the one dropping bombs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll see that in a moment. And wasn't there a fighting plane, possibly a MIG, which was flying over and possibly shooting at people as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So what did you see the fighter plane doing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a fast plane. These are slow planes and I saw those. However, had there been a MIG, I would have had to see it and hear it. I couldn't have missed it. There were no big, fast planes flying over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to the planes shortly but just dealing with the biplane now, we are going to see a section where what appears to be a bomb is dropped from the plane. And we hear a woman saying, [B/C/S spoken], there it is, and then an impact. That's at 4750. Yes. We'll start slightly before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now we saw just then the jolting, a jolting movement a moment ago. Isn't what we've seen a bomb being dropped, a dust cloud being thrown up and even the impact jolting your camera or something of that nature? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No way. It was very far from the camera and I didn't even hear the explosion on that occasion. On another part of the tape, you can see bombs being dropped and explosions. As for this, no. I wouldn't say it was an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe that wasn't the best section to show you. Do you accept that you saw the impact of bombs falling in Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] get that last Friday. He did testify, Mr. Jones, that some bombs may not have exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes so it follows that some did explode.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, some did, obviously, and we saw. We had seen this tape anyway. So please go ahead and ask him any questions you like of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you estimate how many bombs were dropped that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Less than ten, more than 20, 50?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't want to play around with numbers because I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we heard a person earlier on the tape saying, if there are Ustasha there, they must be crazy. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when that person was referring to Ustashas, he was referring to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just for our benefit, that's in fact a rather ugly term used to describe Muslims by Serbs sometimes, isn't it, comparing them to World War II Nazis?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand the situation. One side called the other Ustasha and the other side called the others Chetniks. That was the usual way of referring to the other side at the time. It was not derogatory. It was just a normal term that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Serbs also called themselves Chetniks, though, don't they, in terms of there being Chetnik units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm telling you the Muslims called all the Serbs Chetniks and the Serbs called all the Muslims Ustasha, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it was simply to say that there were Serbs who called themselves Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it didn't mean anything derogatory. It was just a way of designating the side you were on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But when the person said, if there were Ustasha there they must be crazy, he was recognising, wasn't he, that it must have been extremely terrible situation for any Muslims who were in Sikiric with bombs falling on them, et cetera. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that's what he meant but I don't know what he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already answered the question but clearly that was a question that called for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you at all. That's why I allowed it. I knew what your objection would be but that's -- it's the witness's understanding of what the words uttered by the other person meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Okanovic, you told us on Friday that you at the time knew that the Muslims were desperately short of food, the Muslims on the other side of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that but I assumed that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] you aware at the time that at Bratunac, Serbs, even including civilians and including civilian women, were blocking aid convoys bound for Srebrenica, in order to deny them food?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I just want to go back to the planes briefly. The planes you told us on Friday flew down from the direction of Bratunac and you showed how they went over the road from Bratunac. Would it be correct to say that they were close to the Drina pretty much the whole time that you were observing them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were taking off somewhere near Bratunac. There was some kind of auxiliary airport built there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're aware of an airfield, there being an impromptu airfield in Bratunac at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was one. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you also aware that planes were flying from Serbia proper over into Bosnia, in this action?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No they weren't flying from Serbia or you weren't aware?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't flying from there because at that point we were angry with our forces for not helping or for not coming to the Drina later on to protect us because we were afraid. And that's why we organised those village guards, as I said. In the municipality we protested against our own leaders who did nothing, although there was no cause, as it turned out, for us to fear because nothing actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. It was really just to establish this: That these planes you saw, isn't it right that when you were observing them they were either above you at one point in Vrhpolje or in your village or above the Drina or above Sikiric? They were in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a small area, and when it was turning round, it flew above us. Also, there were being shot at and probably that was the reason why they fled to this side. At one point, I thought one of the planes had been hit and maybe it was hit. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the planes were clearly audible, weren't they, were they were even over Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Simply this: That you could hear them one kilometre away in Vrhpolje when they were flying over Sikiric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right that this was from around 9.00 in the morning onwards, that at least a plane or planes were flying above Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, yes. Not continuously. But intermittently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. You told us on Friday that you first saw houses burning and then planes arriving afterwards. How many houses had you in fact noticed as burning before a plane arrived? Can you estimate?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You can't excludes the possibility, can you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses that had been set on fire in the morning were burning throughout this time. I don't recall any houses being set on fire later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But do you accept that a certain number of houses might have started burning after the planes arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that was the case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You can't tell us how many houses you saw burning before planes arrived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered that question, Mr. Jones, already, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Also just to clarify one matter. On Friday, you were shown a shot from this video and you could see a plane drop a bomb into the woods and you said the plane has dropped bombs in the woods. Just to confirm, that was -- you were referring just to that particular still of the video, correct? It's not as if all the bombs were being dropped in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't mean that all the bombs were dropped there. I took shots of almost all of the bombs that were dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that answers also your previous question as to how many bombs were dropped on that day, Mr. Jones. More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can go back and count all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as the number of planes that were flying above Sikiric that day, we've had reference to a biplane and to another plane. Isn't it a fact that there were more than two planes, but in fact three or four planes that you observed that day? Did you recall that it was only two or could it have been more?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw one in the air, and I tell you, at the time I was making the videotape, I didn't even notice that the planes were different. It was only later on when I looked at the tape that I saw that the planes were different. At the time, I didn't pay attention to what kind of plane it was. It was only later on I saw that they were different planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now you also mentioned an armoured vehicle on the Serb side, rather on the side of Serbia proper, which was also shooting in the afternoon. I want to ask you, you noticed that in the afternoon but do you exclude the possibility that it was firing from that position before then and that you had simply not noticed it? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain it wasn't there earlier and I'm sure it arrived from the Bosnian side. It wasn't there either before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's an armoured vehicle which arrived from the Bosnian side, took up a position on the side of Serbia and then shot back towards Sikiric? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what type of vehicle it was and whether it was an armoured vehicle. It was quite far away. It is on my videotape and if you can use the tape to recognise the type of vehicle, well that's fine, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, well we may come to that because there is reference to a tank, in fact, on your video. That the child is saying, "There is a tank." If you recall that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. But when the child said it was a tank, probably the child thought all vehicles were tanks or vehicles of that type. I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think while we are on the subject we may as well look at that part of the video. I think it's the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record we are looking at 51 -- we started the video rolling at 51.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's that section of the video, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and the video was stopped at 53.08.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the child says there is a tank.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear those comments, but I don't know whether it was a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We've actually finished with that video for the time being and probably for good, P316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also said on Friday that you didn't think that there were Bosnian Serb soldiers based in Bjelovac or Sikiric. Now would you agree that that was purely an assumption on your part based on the fact that it was a small village and you didn't see the point?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any. Those are assumptions. I know that they were undisciplined and didn't respect their guard duty and I assumed that they were not in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're aware that Bjelovac is on the road from Skelani to Bratunac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that it's the only road or the only direct road connecting those two places and that it goes all along the Drina past all the villages?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you aware at the time that there were VRS brigades in both Skelani and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Bratunac, but as for Skelani, that's a bit further away and I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware in December of 1992 that there was a brigade in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know about military units. I know there were troops there but I don't know what kind of unit it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how many kilometres is it from Bjelovac to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five kilometres, four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you agree, having served in the military and knowing perhaps something of those things, that the road, that road on the Drina was of considerable strategic significance at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But in fact you never went to Bjelovac during 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't the reason why you didn't go because there was shooting going on over in that area the whole time and it was considered very dangerous? Sorry, you said [B/C/S spoken] but it wasn't interpreted. If that could be interpreted. If you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was unsafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you give us any idea of the frequency that you would hear shooting on the ordinary side of the Drina? Was it on a weekly basis, monthly basis, daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, it was on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's from April 1992, from the start of the war, until December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was also shooting when some kind of actions were being carried out, but there was also shooting for no reason at all. People celebrating being rowdy, they would throw bombs in the River Drina. People behaved irresponsibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in Vrhpolje, or in your area in any event, you were very much aware, weren't you, that Serbs were sending their families out of the area precisely because it was a war zone?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody sent anyone from Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not from Vrhpolje but the people were coming from the other side of the Drina over to Serbia to evacuate their families because it wasn't considered safe there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact would you agree, if you know, that probably most people, most Serbian families, on the other side of the Drina sent their women and children away at the start of the war? Sent them over to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes, but later on, they came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes the other side of the Drina seems a rather large area to me. If we can pinpoint, if Mr. Jones is able to, exactly what areas he is referring to. If we are just referring to the other side then it seems a fairly large area to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct, yes. Mr. Jones, I think if you abided by what Ms. Richardson is suggesting, we would be in a position, in a better position, to understand exactly the extent of your question and of the answer that we got from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When I refer to the other side of the Drina, I'm referring perhaps -- tell me if you understood me or not, to the villages from Bratunac downwards towards Skelani which were across the river from you and of which you were aware; in other words, Bjelovac, I suppose Fakovici, and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about the area parallel to Vrhpolje. A few families, not all of them, but a few families, crossed over before the war started and later on they went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Including families from Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, but I don't know any specific particular family from Bjelovac who crossed over the Drina with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, during 1992, in this period which we have been considering when you were hearing shots from the other side of the Drina but not venturing over there, did you nonetheless see tanks, transporters and other military hardware travelling back and forth on that road?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't observe that. I have no idea. It wasn't an area where there was a lot of army communication. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown Defence Exhibit D255, with the usher's assistance, please. For the record, the ERN is 02158988 to 02158997. It's a document of the Office of the Military Prosecutor of the VRS dated 13 October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'd ask you, Mr. Okanovic, to turn to a page which ends 8997, look at the top right-hand corner, 02158997. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see the name Pejic Milorad, in capitals, halfway down?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that refers, doesn't it, to him as a member of the Armoured Mechanised Company in Bjelovac and we see the date is the 14th of September 1992, that an incident occurred. Do you see all that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I return to my question in the hope that seeing that seeing that, seeing that apparently there was an armoured mechanised company in Bjelovac might have jolted your memory as to whether you did see tanks and transporters across the Drina in Bjelovac and Sikiric during the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with this case. If I'd seen any of that, I would have taped it, but I'm sure I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know Nikola Petrovic from Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if I saw the person, I'd recognise the person, but the name doesn't ring a bell. I knew a lot of people in Bratunac because I lived there for a while. I'm not sure if I know what his position was, but certainly the name tells me nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In relation to that, if we were to show you houses in Bjelovac and ask you who their owners would be, that's not something you could help us with, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be very difficult, very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to just a few more questions on the action on the 14th of December 1992, you told us how fighting between Serbs and Muslims, as you assumed, went on all day. Was it your understanding that this wasn't a walkover but a fierce, two-way fight which therefore lasted all day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't fierce. It was quite a laugh. It was completely disorganised on both sides. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So again when you said that it was Muslim forces who were involved in Bjelovac on the 14th of December 1992 that again was an assumption on your part wasn't it based on the fact that it was a Serb village and you couldn't imagine Serbs attacking Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not a Serb village. It used to be a mixed village before the war. Once the war began, they split up and then the Serbs remained in the village. I assume it was the Serbs who remained in the village but I can't confirm that either. If the Serbs were the ones who remained, that means that the Muslims were the ones who attacked them because there would not have been anyone else around to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's consistent, that assumption is consistent with Muslim civilians going into Bjelovac rather than forces or troops, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on the basis that this is a question that calls for speculation by the witness. I think he's already testified that there was fighting and he doesn't know who was involved and to put the question to him about Muslim civilians going into the village, I think it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we are all clear then if he doesn't know who was involved then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained and in any case, I don't think you can go around this, Mr. Jones. I mean you have already got more than one statement on this matter from the witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now you told us that you assumed it was Serbs who remained in Bjelovac, not Muslims. Can you explain why you made that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made that assumption based on what I heard on the radio, on what people said. Stuff like that, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, these Bosnian Serbs would cross the Drina to go and get food. That sort of thing. This means that there were Bosnian Serbs on the other side and not Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't it much more positive information you received than that? Weren't you in fact aware that there was ethnic cleansing of the Muslims in their villages all along the Drina at the start of 1992 and that the Muslims had been expelled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was ethnic cleansing on both sides. Where there were Muslims there were no Serbs and vice versa. That's as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One final question on the action the 14th of December 1992. As to how each individual house got damaged, you're not able to say, are you, whether rather than being deliberately set on fire, they were either damaged by a bomb from a plane or damaged by a zolja, by some other means, other than human agency. That's not something you can say, is it -- is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour my objection is to the reference to the bomb. I think the witness has already testified that he did not see a bomb cause damage to the houses and they were in fact burning prior to the bomb. So my objection is solely with respect to that part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you, Ms. Richardson. I think you've made your point and it's a valid point. At the same time, no harm done because the witness's answer, as I expected it to be, does not really throw much light on what could have caused the damage or the fire. Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do not to clarify on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're not excluding the possibility that bombs caused damage to property --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we are in the realm of pure speculation. I mean, he's told you that he can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine, Your Honour. It's a distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he can not tell, he cannot include or exclude any possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that in fact you filmed more than the scenes which we saw on Friday, that in fact you started filming area at about a quarter to nine and that we haven't seen that section of the video?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that was recorded has been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We are going to show the witness part of P428. It's already a Prosecution exhibit. We have added just for convenience subtitles and we have a transcript as well of that section, which we will distribute the transcript and we realised perhaps belatedly but that although this is a Prosecution exhibit, we should make copies of the DVD with the subtitles for the parties and we will certainly do that in the next day or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and if you want to give it a Defence exhibit number, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is nothing impeding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will play this first bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could have a look, Mr. Okanovic, and see if you recall that that's also footage which you shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make a comment. It's clear there are houses on fire but they are not firing yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise that as being shot from your -- as being filmed from your house, from the building in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very difficult for me to pin down in terms of location, but I assume it must be the same camera. I assume I was the one who taped this or it may have been someone else too but what is quite obvious is that the planes have not taken off yet here. But it must have been me. I was the one who taped this, because I was the one with the radio and the voices that we have just heard are talking over the radio. So now that I've analysed the situation I can say that I was the one who taped it. And it is only now that they are saying something about planes being about to take off. This is from Bratunac, from the centre. That much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We will play on in a moment and I'll have some questions to ask about it. You might also recognise the video perhaps from the brief segment we saw of what looked like a western or some film which appears briefly. But in any event, if you could -- if that is what you filmed, then I'll have some questions after we finish playing it. Sorry, that is the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly it's right, isn't it, that the people we hear speaking are Serbs as one can tell from the context, the content from the use of the Ekavian dialect and from the hard ch?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they were Serbs, yes. Positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the -- what you recorded you heard on the radio, would this be the walkie-talkie device which you had with you or some other device?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the walkie-talkie.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as an expert in radio communications, hearing the quality, the slight echoes and what not, could you confirm that this is interception of a military communication by radio?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- usually I would suggest, Ms. Richardson, to wait until the witness answers the question but I'm anticipating the objection. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is based on the fact that I don't think it has been established that this witness is an expert in radio communications and as such may not be able to answer this question and it's if he does it's only based on any -- on speculation on his part. I think that there has been no testimony that he's an expert in radio communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's only one part or one side of the story maybe. Let him answer the question. Are you in a position, Mr. Okanovic, to tell us whether this radio interception or radio conversation that you overheard and taped basically was military communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was no military communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are excluding it being a military communication? And if you are, why are you so categorical? On what grounds can you be so precise, so specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't rule out the possibility that the person speaking was someone from the army, but this was certainly not a military channel because this frequency was used by ham radios and these people were using ham radio frequencies and not military frequencies. I'm talking about this particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to come to these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, as far as the expertise which you have is concerned, isn't it right that in fact you have considerable technical background with radios, including ability to fix equipment and to use what I think is called a goniometer? Is that correct? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during the war, before you had the technology and the expertise to eavesdrop on communications including by decoding communications? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You referred to goniometer a while ago. You probably don't know what that means and yet you're implying that I had it. And secondly, decoding, I'm not quite clear what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You did catch me out. Can you explain to us what a goniometer is?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it in the simplest possible terms, for that you need to have an a system of radio devices in place, a connected system with antennas pointed or trained in the right direction both horizontally and vertically so that it can pinpoint precise locations and these two independent systems then communicate and provide accurate coordinates. I mean two lines and at the point of intersection of these two lines, that's where you find the radio device. So all I could do was put together a directional aerial to be better able to eavesdrop on the other side but I could not get a clear direction. There wasn't something that I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that that's fairly sophisticated technology and that you know how to use it? If you had the equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I wouldn't be able to use it. If someone trained me, perhaps I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that helps clarify to a certain extent the expertise this witness has.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to this conversation you told us it was on an open channel, but of course the content is of a military nature, isn't it? We are talking about military units and troops and attacks.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can draw that conclusion yourself, whether yes or no. Please don't make me analyse that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I won't ask to you analyse it but I would ask you to confirm that the transcript which you have in front of you and we can replay what that reflects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, is whatever answer that the witness will give you going to change the substance or the nature of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I think we do need some confirmation that the transcript is accurate, that it accurately reflects what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's something different. It's completely different to what you're asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My last question is for him to confirm that the transcript accurately reflects what is being said. I'll ask him to do that because we need to do that with a witness. We'll replay the video and he can look at the transcript as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to -- in fact, just as a sort of preface we are going to replay the video again, Mr. Okanovic. If you could confirm or tell us if it's wrong in any way, the content of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How is he going to tell us whether the transcript is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, I see. All right. He has got a copy of it, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Let's go -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may make a comment. A while ago counsel put it to me that they were speaking Ijkavian but they weren't. They spoke Ekavian, which has been noted in the transcript. Therefore, these are Bosnian Serbs. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you and their mentioning [B/C/S spoken] and [B/C/S spoken]. From your radio intercepts, are you aware or from other information, that those are Serb units, [B/C/S spoken] and [B/C/S spoken]?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you confirm --

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not something that I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You followed the transcript as we watched the clip. Do you confirm that what's written there accurately reflects what is being said?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I may come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones, please. Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just before we go on, since certain villages are mentioned, could we be shown on a map where these villages are located in relation to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We did have the Prosecution map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: We have a map here, yes. P536.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, P536. Can that be placed on the ELMO? Actually, perhaps what is the best course is if we play the video and just freeze it each time a place name comes up and the witness can point it out. One moment, Witness. We will ask you about the villages as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll -- it will take us less time and it will be easier if -- because there aren't a large number of places mentioned here. So let's put the map on the ELMO, please, and let's take them -- where is Pirici, please? Could you show us Pirici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could [inaudible] be permitted to assist the witness since the object is just for us to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, it is, Pirici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the witness points to Pirici on the map, which is at 35, 35 minutes to the south, at the south of Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is also we just saw Bjelovacka Rijeka is referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should all be part of Bjelovac, as far as I know. These are mere hamlets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And Rijeka means a river, doesn't it? Bjelovacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes but I don't know exactly which one it is, whether it's the one going towards Sase or this creek over here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] is also mentioned. Isn't it right that that's also part of Sikiric? It may not appear on the map but just from your knowledge, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Kunjarac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Kunjarac, yes. There is a hill right behind Bjelovac, and it should be this one. Yes, this one right here. I know because there is a water works that supplies Bratunac. That was built here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness puts a spot, plots a spot on the man, a circle, right above Biljaca. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Loznicka Rijeka is also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then this could be Loznicka Rijeka and Bjelovacka Rijeka. If that was the name. Could be this one, because Loznicka is right here. But I'm not sure about this. You must understand I'm not entirely certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on this conversation, and I'm asking you based on your experience as a radio ham, that you agree that what this conversation reflects is aircraft being scrambled, being given coordinates and told where to target?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's obvious, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's at 8.43, 8.44 in the morning, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS OKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've come to an end of one subject. Perhaps this will be a good time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will have the break now. 25 minutes, yes. Yes, I hinted to Mr. Jones and I think he agrees with it that this part of the video from whichever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that you tender it separately as your own exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Together with this would be point 1. I don't know the sequential number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've lost track myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't remember either. So what would be the next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D271 and the transcript would be 271.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if need be, I don't think there is any dispute, but we can easily show that it's part of 428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that's being contested, I don't know. Is that being contested, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Although I have to say that the witness has said that there were other people videotaping and he's not certain but I think it's a possibility that it's his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you wants to pursue the matter, perhaps you can ask him that -- is that very short clip which is obviously an interruption in the video which shows part of a film that must have been recorded before, if we can show it to him and he can perhaps tell us about it, whether he remembers. But I got the impression that on second thoughts the witness is quite sure that this video was shot by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, so did I, Your Honour. But just so that we are just to be as accurate as we can be perhaps we can ask him as well if that part -- portion of the tape that shows that clip sort of confirms 100 per cent his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. We will show it to him after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I don't think there is any harm done in being secure about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The Prosecution can put questions in re-examination. I don't want the Prosecution to be putting my questions in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's resume at 11.00 sharp, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the witness to -- my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your client hasn't sat down as yet. I understand there is a problem or something you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wanted the witness to be kept out just briefly there is a clarification and an objection, if you like, about this -- concerning this video. Now, I listed evidence from this witness as to whether the first part of the video was something which he taped or not, and I asked questions and he eventually, it's page 29, line 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He gave the impression --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, in fact the end of it was "I analysed the situation. I can say I was the one who taped it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At the close of the first -- before the first break, my point, which I rose was simply a technical point that this extract was an extract of a Prosecution exhibit - in other words, there is P428 and we had just taken a bit of it and put subtitles on it. And it was simply to find out whether the Prosecution contested that in order to avoid the exercise. At that point, my learned friend, Ms. Richardson, sought to revisit the area of whether this witness was sure that he had taped that part of the video. Completely different question, firstly, sought to put a question which is better saved for re-examination as to whether he's sure. But, worse, suggested to the witness, because she said, what Ms. Richardson said is he's not certain but it's a possibility that it's his, as to that extract. So in other words, misstated the evidence because that's not the evidence; but then clearly suggested to this witness that they don't -- the Prosecution doesn't want him to be sure that he taped that clip. Certainly the witness hearing that might think, perhaps I shouldn't be so sure about this. It's completely inappropriate. It amounts to trying to discuss the evidence before -- in front of the witness and I've had the sense to keep the witness out when we discuss the evidence and I trust that my learned friends won't do anything like that again because it could contaminate the evidence this witness if he gets the impression that he should be unsure. If Ms. Richardson wants to put questions in re-examination that's the appropriate moment for it. I wanted to state that objection on the record firstly, but also because we will now - because the Prosecution hasn't been clear about this - we will demonstrate that this is part of P428. We can even do it without the witness although we I think we should do it with the witness simply by cueing that one part of the anomalous part of the video where there is the scene from some film and show that that's on P428 and continues on the rest of the video which we saw in P316. I want to make that completely clear because I don't want my learned friend popping up and objecting and suggesting any more to this witness that maybe he didn't film this section. That's not the exercise. The exercise is simply to show that our exhibit is part of P428. As I said, we don't even really need the witness for that demonstration. So I would ask my learned friend not to do anything like that again and also not to, as happened one or twice this morning, interrupt witnesses when they are answering. Your Honour has been quite clear that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't allowed Ms. Richardson to interrupt, in any case. Yes, and I think as regards the point raised, yes what are your comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour I'll keep it brief. First of all, I think it's -- since we are a number of us are from adversarial systems when an objection is -- when a question is posed that is objectionable it is the right of the Prosecution to raise to his feet, to not pop but to raise to its feet and lodge an objection to the Court. And Your Honour, I have been quite, I think, mindful when you have indicated to me not to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's skip this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Secondly Your Honour, I would just say with respect to my response regarding our objection to the video, it was in direct response to Your Honour's question if the Prosecution was objecting. And I think it was in this discourse that I indicated that I had some concerns about portions of the tape and just to ensure that this was in fact the videotape of the witness. Because I did not recollect as accurately as Mr. Jones just pointed out, clearly because he looked at LiveNote that the witness was emphatically certain that it was his. So I was trying to simply get to that point and not in any way to influence the witness's testimony. I think this witness is -- will be very honest about that. So I in no way tried to influence his testimony. When Your Honour is finished, I'd like to raise a point myself on another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In actual fact the only problem is that you should have stopped the moment I pointed out to you that the witness had earlier on in his testimony made it clear that he recollected -- he remembered this video to have been shot by him. But anyway, I consider the chapter closed. And if you have any other matter to -- you would like to raise please do it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My the point that I'd like to raise is a matter that I observed myself during the time that we were in recess when counsel, Mr. Jones, attempted to access the computer of the legal officer, which I think is inappropriate behaviour for either of these parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which legal officer?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The legal officer in front of you, Your Honour. I'm pointing it out to the Court Your Honour so everybody can be aware that I think, first of all, that this is inappropriate behaviour and I don't think that this should have been attempted and not saying Mr. Jones was able to access it, but he did attempt to. And I did raise the matter with him that I thought that was not a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this your? What happened? One moment, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I say this is an absolutely scandalous accusation that the Prosecution is making. It's the sort of tit-for-tat, it seems, for the fact that I raised a proper matter. But I'm practically lost for words because I can't believe the Prosecution would actually try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, tell us what happened because she made a very serious accusation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not true tell us what your version of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. After the after the break we realised that we didn't have access to LiveNote. Because of using the videos I couldn't have LiveNote here. It hadn't been connected on that computer I needed to check precisely what the witness had said on this subject of the video. I went to the registry bench, thinking perhaps I could look there on LiveNote. I realised it was inappropriate and I went over to the stenographers instead. The stenographers were here in the courtroom. Ms. Richardson was here. Ms. Henry-Frijlink was here. They were two feet away from me. I said I'm going to check LiveNote on the Registry bench. Ms. Richardson did in fact say, I don't think that's appropriate. I immediately went over, as the stenographers can confirm, the gentleman in the corner, and I said can you please check this reference and he very kindly obliged. As I left the courtroom, I saw the legal officer and I said to her, By the way I was going to try to get LiveNote on your computer and I realised I shouldn't do so. I informed her specifically during the break that I had briefly floated in the direction of her computer and then thought better of it and gone to the stenographer. The stenographer can confirm that he helped me find that section of the transcript. Anyone can confirm that I didn't touch the computer and the fact that Ms. Richardson has raised it is really beneath her and beneath me. I'm frankly scandalised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: May I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Certainly this is not a tit-for-tat situation. In fact I approached the usher prior to us coming into the courtroom and told her I was going to raise the matter and that I did not want the witness to be brought in. I raised the matter with the senior trial attorney, Your Honour, Mr. Wubben, and we decided we would raise this matter. And I had no idea that Mr. Jones was going to raise the matter that he did. So it's certainly not a tit for tat. And Mr. Jones was poised at the computer when I indicated to him this was not a good idea and there were witnesses here, Your Honour, who can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We are suspending the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say just one thing. If I were going to accuses the computer of your legal officer, to do that in front of two members of the Prosecution bench, in front of a lot of witnesses would be, frankly, completely absurd. There is an absolute storm in a tea cup. I briefly drifted over, thinking I could check the LiveNote, because I was in a hurry to find out what the transcript was. I went over and got it from another source. I think it's deeply unfair and deeply unprofessional for Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's finished. No more arguments, please, Mr. Jones and Ms. Richardson. The matter is closed for the time being. We are going out to discuss it very briefly. We will be back in about two minutes. --- Break taken at 11.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, which one of the stenographers did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The gentleman, all right. So I think that you will need to answer our question and at the same time keep typing. So you heard what Mr. Jones said earlier on. THE COURT REPORTER: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you confirm his statement? THE COURT REPORTER: Yes, he came over and asked to see the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And? Yes. And what happened? THE COURT REPORTER: I showed him the LiveNote and he wrote in longhand what he was reading on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at the time, who was present in the courtroom? THE COURT REPORTER: I'm sorry, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Jones approaching the legal officers? THE COURT REPORTER: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't. And do you remember an exchange of words between Ms. Richardson and Mr. Jones? THE COURT REPORTER: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Jones at any time touching or using any of the -- desktops or notebooks that we have here? THE COURT REPORTER: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think at this point in time, the matter rests here. However, we would like to make it clear that if either of you have got a problem and you need to access the LiveNote because it is not readily available on the system that you have at your disposal, that you approach either the Registrar or the other party for that matter, but that you do not try to use any of the sets that we have here, particularly the legal officer attached to Chamber, of course, who is here at our disposal and not at your disposal. However we are satisfied that nothing really wrong did occur on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I first went to that laptop and there wasn't LiveNote on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
